name: Strange Array
description: Vasya has an array of $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$. Vasya thinks that all numbers in his array are strange for some reason. To calculate how strange the $$$i$$$-th number is, Vasya created the following algorithm. He chooses a subsegment $$$a_l, a_{l+1}, \ldots, a_r$$$, such that $$$1 \le l \le i \le r \le n$$$, sort its elements in increasing order in his head (he can arrange equal elements arbitrary). After that he finds the center of the segment. The center of a segment is the element at position $$$(l + r) / 2$$$, if the length of the segment is odd, and at position $$$(l + r + 1) / 2$$$ otherwise. Now Vasya finds the element that was at position $$$i$$$ before the sorting, and calculates the distance between its current position and the center of the subsegment (the distance between the elements with indices $$$j$$$ and $$$k$$$ is $$$|j - k|$$$). The strangeness of the number at position $$$i$$$ is the maximum distance among all suitable choices of $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$. Vasya wants to calculate the strangeness of each number in his array. Help him to do it.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 200\,000$$$) — the size of the array. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le n$$$) — Vasya's array.
output_specification: Print a single line with $$$n$$$ numbers. The $$$i$$$-th of them must be equal to the strangeness of the $$$i$$$-th element of the array.
approach_summary: Maintain prefix sums and dynamic point updates via Fenwick tree using lowbit operations (i & -i) in O(log N) time and O(N) space.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1539F — Strange Array [70. BIT / Fenwick Tree]
topic_editorial.summary: Point updates and range prefix queries with Fenwick Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Every integer $i$ has a unique binary decomposition. Index $i$ in a Binary Indexed Tree stores the cumulative sum of the interval $(i - \text{lowbit}(i), i]$, allowing logarithmic traversal via $i \mathrel{+}= (i \mathbin{\&} -i)$ and $i \mathrel{-}= (i \mathbin{\&} -i)$.
